title: Bellman-Ford
tagline: Shortest paths that tolerate negative edges — and detect negative cycles.

intuition.analogy: Rumours spreading through an office: after one round everyone one desk away knows; after two rounds, two desks away. After V−1 rounds, the news has had time to travel the longest possible simple path to everyone.
paragraphs: Dijkstra's greedy choice fails with negative edges. Bellman-Ford instead brute-forces correctness: it relaxes every edge repeatedly. After k rounds, all shortest paths using at most k edges are correct.
A shortest path in a graph with V vertices uses at most V−1 edges, so V−1 rounds of relaxing all edges settles every distance.

Bonus: if a V-th round still improves some distance, a negative-weight cycle exists (reachable from the source). That detection ability is unique and valuable — e.g. arbitrage detection in currency graphs.
intuition.keyIdea: Relax all edges V−1 times; one more improving round signals a negative cycle.

steps.title: Relax V−1 times
steps.detail: Repeat V−1 rounds; in each, for every edge (u,v,w): if dist[u]+w < dist[v], update dist[v].

steps.title: Detect negative cycles
steps.detail: Run one extra round. Any edge that still relaxes proves a reachable negative cycle.

problems.title: Cheapest Flights Within K Stops
problems.statement: Cheapest price with at most K stops.
problems.hint: Bellman-Ford limited to K+1 relaxation rounds.

approach: We want the cheapest price using at most K stops, i.e. at most K+1 edges. Bellman-Ford naturally bounds the number of edges by the number of relaxation rounds.
Run K+1 rounds; in each round relax every flight using costs from the previous round only (snapshot), so a path never uses more than the allowed number of edges.

problems.title: Network Delay Time
problems.statement: Time to reach all nodes from a source.
problems.hint: Bellman-Ford also solves it (slower than Dijkstra).

approach: Single-source shortest path from node k; the answer is the maximum finishing distance (or -1 if some node is unreachable).
Bellman-Ford relaxes all edges V-1 times. The signal time is the largest shortest-distance over all nodes.

problems.title: Detect Negative Cycle
problems.statement: Determine if a weighted digraph has a negative cycle.

approach: After V-1 rounds of relaxation all shortest paths are settled if there is no negative cycle. A Vth round that still relaxes an edge proves a reachable negative cycle exists.
Start all distances at 0 (a virtual source connected to every node) so the detection covers the whole graph.

problems.title: Arbitrage Detection
problems.hint: Use −log(rate) as weights; a negative cycle means arbitrage.

approach: An arbitrage cycle multiplies rates to > 1. Take negative logarithms of rates: a product > 1 becomes a sum < 0, so arbitrage is exactly a negative cycle.
Run Bellman-Ford on the -log(rate) graph and detect a negative cycle.
